docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
KOR-ee, from the greek Κόρη, the queen of the underworld, daughter of Zeus and Demeter. Kore is a numerical tool to study the core flow within rapidly rotating planets or other rotating fluids contained within near-spherical boundaries.

Kore solves the linear Navier-Stokes equation and, optionally, the induction equation and the heat and composition equations (Boussinesq approximation) for a viscous, incompressible and electrically conducting fluid in a rotating spherical shell or full sphere. An externally imposed magnetic field can be included. So can a solid inner core, which can be electrically insulating, conducting, perfectly conducting, or covered by a thin conducting layer. The mantle can be insulating or have a thin conducting layer at its base, and both the mantle and the inner core can rotate in response to the torques the fluid exerts on them.

Kore assumes all dynamical variables to oscillate in a harmonic fashion. The oscillation frequency can be imposed externally, as is the case when doing forced motion studies (e.g. tidal forcing or libration), or it can be obtained as part of the solution to an eigenvalue problem. The eigenmodes Kore finds include the inertial modes (the restoring force is the Coriolis force), the gravity modes (buoyancy), the torsional Alfvén modes (the Lorentz force) and the magneto-Archimedes-Coriolis (MAC) modes (a combination of the three).

Kore's distinctive feature is the use of a very efficient spectral method employing Gegenbauer (also known as ultraspherical) polynomials as a basis in the radial direction. This approach leads to sparse matrices representing the differential equations, as opposed to dense matrices, as in traditional Chebyshev collocation methods. Sparse matrices have a smaller memory footprint and are more suitable for systematic core flow studies at extremely low viscosities (or small Ekman numbers). The matrices are solved in parallel with PETSc, SLEPc and MUMPS.

Kore is free for everyone to use under the GPL v3 license. Too often in the scientific literature the numerical methods used are presented with enough detail to guarantee reproducibility, but only in principle. Without access to the actual implementation of those methods, which would require a significant amount of work and time to develop, readers are left effectively without the possibility to reproduce or verify the results presented. This leads to very slow scientific progress. We share our code to avoid this.

If this code is useful for your research, we invite you to cite the relevant papers (coming soon) and hope that you can also contribute to the project.

docs.title: Background magnetic field
docs.text:
With magnetic = 1, Kore solves for a small magnetic field perturbation \(\mathbf{b}\) on top of a steady, imposed background field \(\mathbf{B}_0\). The background field is axisymmetric and poloidal:

\[ \mathbf{B}_0 = c_{norm}\, \nabla\times\nabla\times\left( h(r)\, Y_l^0(\theta)\, \mathbf{r} \right), \]

where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the position vector, \(Y_l^0\) is a Schmidt semi-normalised spherical harmonic (\(Y_1^0 = \cos\theta\)), and \(c_{norm}\) is set by cnorm. The radial component is \(B_{0r} = c_{norm}\, l(l+1)\, h\, Y_l^0 / r\). The field enters the Lorentz force and the induction term of the linearised equations, the magnetic torques on the boundaries, and spin_doctor's diagnostics.

docs.title: Field shapes
docs.text:
B0 selects the radial function \(h(r)\):

B0 \(l\) \(h(r)\) Notes 'axial' 1 \(r/2\) Uniform field along the rotation axis, \(\mathbf{B}_0 = c_{norm}\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Imposed from outside the core. It has no cylindrical-radial component, so it supports no torsional waves. The default. 'dipole' 1 \(1/(2r^2)\) Point dipole at the centre, current-free in the fluid. Needs an inner core (ricb > 0). 'G21 dipole' 1 \(r/6 - r^3/10\) Dipole made by currents in the fluid (Gerick et al. 2021, GJI). 'Luo_S1' 1 \((5 - 3r^2)\, r\) Luo & Jackson (2022, Proc. R. Soc. A) field S1. Same shape as 'G21 dipole' (30 times larger). 'Luo_S2' 2 \((157 - 296 r^2 + 143 r^4)\, r^2\) Luo & Jackson (2022) quadrupolar field S2. 'FDM' B0_l spherical Bessel functions, see below Poloidal free magnetic decay mode (Zhang & Fearn 1994, 1995; Schmitt 2012).

The free decay mode is \(h = j_l(\beta r)\) in a full sphere (Gubbins & Roberts 1987), and \(h = j_l(\beta r)\, y_{l-1}(\beta) - j_{l-1}(\beta)\, y_l(\beta r)\) in a shell (Zhang & Fearn 1995), with \(j_l\) and \(y_l\) the spherical Bessel functions. \(\beta\) is the decay-mode wavenumber, found by a root search started from beta (default 3); the value found is written to params.dat as beta_actual. B0_l (default 1) is the degree of the mode.

The fields with odd \(l\) are equatorially antisymmetric and 'Luo_S2' is symmetric. The symmetry of \(\mathbf{b}\) is that of the flow (symm) times that of \(\mathbf{B}_0\).

docs.title: The field inside the inner core: B0_ic
docs.text:
'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1' and 'Luo_S2' are defined for a full sphere. With an inner core (ricb > 0) they do not match a potential field at the ICB, so part of the electric current that makes them would have to flow inside the inner core, or in a current sheet on the ICB. Nothing keeps such a current steady in a solid inner core of finite conductivity: there is no flow there, hence no electromotive force, and an axisymmetric azimuthal current decays on the inner core's magnetic diffusion time.

B0_ic Effect 'potential' (default) Removes that part of the current. \(h\) becomes \(h + \beta_{ic}\, r^{-(l+1)}\), with \(\beta_{ic} = r_i^{l+1}\,(r_i h' - l h)/(2l+1)\) evaluated at the ICB. The added term carries no current and keeps the CMB matching, so the currents in the fluid are unchanged, and \(\mathbf{B}_0\) continues into the inner core as the potential field \(h(r_i)\,(r/r_i)^l\). This is the self-consistent steady field for an insulating inner core and for any finite inner-core conductivity. 'full sphere' \(h\) unchanged; its currents extend into the inner core. Self-consistent only for a perfectly conducting inner core, or as a snapshot of currents frozen in the inner core.

B0_ic has no effect for a full sphere, nor for 'axial' and 'FDM' (they already match a potential field at the ICB) or 'dipole' (a point source at the centre). For 'Luo_S2' with ricb = 0.35 the change is 10% of the field at the ICB and 1.7% at the CMB, and it lowers the frequency of the S2 torsional mode by about 1% (insulating inner core).

docs.title: A thin conducting wall at the CMB: B0_cmb
docs.text:
With a thin conducting layer at the base of the mantle (mantle = 'TWA', see Inner core and mantle), the background field must satisfy the wall's matching condition too. A steady \(\mathbf{B}_0\) drives no current in the wall, so only the wall's permeability term c_cmb acts on it, not its conductance c1_cmb. The condition at the CMB is

\[ \left(\frac{1}{\mu} + l\,c_{cmb}\right) (r h)' + l\,h = 0 . \] B0_cmb Effect 'wall' (default) Adds \(\alpha\, r^l\) to \(h\), with \(\alpha\) chosen to satisfy the condition. The added term carries no current and keeps the ICB matching of B0_ic, so the currents in the fluid are unchanged. For \(l = 1\) it is a uniform axial field. 'plain' \(h\) unchanged. The field then meets the wall condition only for c_cmb = 0 and mu = 1.

B0_cmb has no effect with an insulating mantle, with c_cmb = 0 and mu = 1, or for 'axial'. For the S2 torsional mode with c1_cmb = 0.015 it raises the frequency by 0.27% at c_cmb = 0.01 and by 5.8% at c_cmb = 0.3.

docs.title: Inner core and mantle
docs.text:
The magnetic boundary conditions describe what lies on the other side of the fluid's boundaries: an electrical insulator, a conductor, or a thin conducting layer. They are set with innercore at the inner core boundary (ICB) and mantle at the core-mantle boundary (CMB). They only matter with magnetic = 1, and innercore only with an inner core (ricb > 0).

On this page the magnetic field perturbation is written, for each spherical harmonic \(Y_l^m\), as

\[ \mathbf{b} = abla imes abla imes\left( f(r)\, Y_l^m\, \mathbf{r} ight) + abla imes\left( g(r)\, Y_l^m\, \mathbf{r} ight), \]

with poloidal scalar \(f\) and toroidal scalar \(g\), and \(F = r f\), \(G = r g\). Primes are radial derivatives, \(r_i\) is the ICB radius ricb, and the CMB radius is 1.

The background field has to be compatible with the boundaries as well. That is handled by B0_ic and B0_cmb, see Background magnetic field.

docs.title: Insulating boundaries
docs.text:
Outside an insulator the field is a potential field, which decays away from the boundary. Matching \(\mathbf{b}\) to it gives

\[ \text{CMB:}\quad (l+1)\,f + r f' = 0, \quad g = 0; \qquad\qquad \text{ICB:}\quad l\,f - r f' = 0, \quad g = 0 . \]

No electric current crosses an insulating boundary, so there is no electromagnetic torque on it.

docs.title: Conducting inner core
docs.text:
With innercore = 'conducting, Chebys' Kore adds the magnetic field inside the inner core, \(\mathbf{b}_i\), to the unknowns, expanded in N_cic Chebyshev polynomials and spherical harmonics up to lmax_cic. The inner core is solid and at rest in the rotating frame, so its field only diffuses:

\[ \partial_t \mathbf{b}_i = (\Omega au)\, E_\eta\, \eta_{i}\, abla^2 \mathbf{b}_i, \qquad \eta_i = rac{1}{\mu_{i2o}\,\sigma_{i2o}}, \]

where \(\eta_i\) is the inner core's magnetic diffusivity relative to the fluid's. At the ICB, the normal field, the tangential \(\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{b}/\mu\) and the tangential electric field are continuous. With subscripts \(o\) (fluid) and \(i\) (inner core), and the permeabilities relative to the fluid's:

\[ f_o = f_i, \qquad (r f_o)' = rac{(r f_i)'}{\mu_{i2o}}, \qquad g_o = rac{g_i}{\mu_{i2o}}, \] \[ (r g_o)' = \eta_i\,(r g_i)', \qquad r^2 abla_l^2 f_o = \eta_i\, r^2 abla_l^2 f_i, \qquad abla_l^2 = rac{d^2}{dr^2} + rac{2}{r} rac{d}{dr} - rac{l(l+1)}{r^2} . \]

The electric field condition has no \(\mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}_0\) term, so it assumes the fluid at the ICB moves with the inner core: use a no-slip ICB (bci = 1) and Ek > 0.

Resolution. N_cic = 64 (the default) is safe for conductivity ratios from \(10^{-4}\) to 1. In the tests behind this default, 16 polynomials put the eigenvalue off by \(1.6 imes10^{-3}\) at sigma_i2o = 1, and 48 gave broken eigenvectors for the modes away from the target at sigma_i2o = \(10^{-2}\). The inner core adds \(2\,n_{ic}\) unknowns, which is cheap: at \(N = 232\) a torsional-mode run took 40 s and 7.8 GB with a conducting inner core, against 22 s and 7.3 GB with a thin wall.

Limits. As sigma_i2o goes to zero the solution converges to the insulating one (linearly in sigma_i2o).

'conducting, Bessel' is the forced-problem version: the inner-core field is taken as \(j_l(k r)\), with \(k = (1-i)\sqrt{\omega/2E_\eta}\) at the forcing frequency \(\omega\), and only the matching conditions at the ICB are added to the matrix. Its ICB condition is flagged in the CHANGELOG as still to be checked.

docs.title: Perfectly conducting inner core
docs.text:
Inside a perfect conductor the field perturbation vanishes. The conditions are \(f = 0\) and a zero tangential electric field at the ICB. With 'perfect conductor, material' the electric field is taken in the frame of the inner core, which gives \(\nabla_l^2 f = 0\) and \((r g)' = 0\). With 'perfect conductor, spatial' it is taken in the rotating frame, which adds the \(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B}_0\) terms. The two are identical with a no-slip ICB.

These two options are not usable at present: they are missing from the list of inner-core conditions in bin/utils.py (ic_bc_list), so every script stops with ValueError: 'perfect conductor, material' is not in list. The boundary conditions themselves are still in bin/assemble.py, with comments saying they need fixing.

docs.title: Thin conducting wall
docs.text:
'TWA' (thin-wall approximation) represents a thin layer of thickness \(h\), conductivity \(\sigma_w\) and permeability \(\mu_w\) between the fluid and an insulator (Roberts, Glatzmaier & Clune 2010). The layer is described by two numbers:

\[ c = \frac{h\,\mu_w}{r_j\,\mu_f}, \qquad c_1 = \frac{h\,\sigma_w}{r_j\,\sigma_f}, \]

where \(r_j\) is the boundary radius and \(\mu_f\), \(\sigma_f\) are the fluid's values. \(c_1\) is the wall-to-fluid conductance ratio and sets the eddy currents in the wall; \(c\) is a magnetic-permeability term. Both are free parameters (c_cmb, c1_cmb at the CMB and c_icb, c1_icb at the ICB). The conditions, which follow Guervilly, Wood & Brummell (2013, appendix A), are

\[ \text{CMB:}\quad \left(\frac{1}{\mu} + l\,c\right) F' + \frac{l}{r}\, F + \frac{c_1}{\mu}\, r\, \mathcal{D}_l F = 0, \qquad G + c_1\, r\, G' = 0, \] \[ \text{ICB:}\quad \left(\frac{1}{\mu} + (l+1)\,c\right) F' - \frac{l+1}{r}\, F - \frac{c_1}{\mu}\, r\, \mathcal{D}_l F = 0, \qquad G - c_1\, r\, G' = 0, \]

with \(\mathcal{D}_l F = F'' - l(l+1)F/r^2 = r\,\nabla_l^2 f\). With \(c = c_1 = 0\) and \(\mu = 1\) they reduce to the insulating conditions. They were checked against the exact free-decay rates of a sphere and a shell bounded by thin walls, to \(10^{-14}\).

The term \(\mathcal{D}_l F\) stands for the wall's \(\partial_t F/\eta\), taken from the fluid next to it. That substitution needs the wall to move with the fluid, so a wall with \(c_1 \neq 0\) needs a no-slip boundary and Ek > 0; assemble.py prints a warning otherwise. With a wall at the CMB, keep B0_cmb = 'wall' (the default) so that the background field satisfies the wall condition too (see Background magnetic field).

docs.title: Electromagnetic torques
docs.text: A conducting layer or inner core lets currents close outside the fluid, and the Lorentz force then exerts an axial torque on the boundary. spin_doctor.py reports it for \(m = 0\), symmetric flows: \(|\Gamma|_{mag}\) for the mantle (with mantle = 'TWA') and \(|\Gamma|_{magIC}\) for the inner core (with 'conducting, Chebys' or 'TWA'). The complex torques are written to magnetic.dat (see Output and postprocessing). With rotdyn = 1 the same torques make the mantle and inner core rotate (see Rotational dynamics).

docs.title: Thin wall or conducting inner core?
docs.text: The thin wall is cheaper to set up, but it is not a substitute for a conducting inner core. When the inner core's field is a skin layer of depth \(\delta = \sqrt{2\eta_i/\omega}\), the conducting inner core acts on the fluid exactly like a thin wall, but with a complex, frequency-dependent conductance, \(c_1 \approx (1-i)\,\delta/2r_i\) for \(\delta \ll r_i\). Kore's thin wall takes a real \(c_1\). In tests with the torsional modes at \(E = 10^{-7}\) and \(10^{-8}\), the best real \(c_1\) still left the eigenvalues 1 to 2% off, with errors of 5 to 15 degrees in the phase of the inner-core torque. The mode in which the inner core and the fluid oscillate together was off by about 20%. Use a conducting inner core when the inner core's electromagnetic coupling matters, and the thin wall for a thin conducting layer such as the base of the mantle.

docs.title: Equations and scaling
docs.text:
Kore solves the linearised equations for small perturbations of a state of rest in the rotating frame: the flow \(\mathbf{u}\), the magnetic field \(\mathbf{b}\) (on top of the imposed background field \(\mathbf{B}_0\), see Background magnetic field), the temperature \( heta\) and the composition \(\xi\) (on top of background profiles \(T(r)\) and \(C(r)\)). The Lorentz force and the induction term are linearised about \(\mathbf{B}_0\):

\[ ( abla imes\mathbf{B}) imes\mathbf{B} \;\longrightarrow\; ( abla imes\mathbf{b}) imes\mathbf{B}_0 + ( abla imes\mathbf{B}_0) imes\mathbf{b}, \qquad abla imes(\mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}) \;\longrightarrow\; abla imes(\mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}_0). \]

Every perturbation varies as \(e^{\lambda t + i m \phi}\). In an eigenvalue problem \(\lambda = \sigma + i\omega\) is unknown, with damping rate \(\sigma\) and frequency \(\omega\). In a forced problem \(\lambda = i\omega\) is the forcing frequency.

docs.title: Non-dimensionalization
docs.text: For numerical convenience we use dimensionless variables when solving the Navier Stokes equation, the induction equation, the heat equation and the composition equation. A non-dimensionalization procedure is always possible thanks to the Buckingham-\(\pi\) theorem. The unit of length \(L\) is the CMB radius.

docs.title: The momentum equation
docs.text:
In a reference frame rotating with angular speed \(\Omega\), the dimensional form of the linear momentum equation (i.e. the Navier-Stokes equation) describing the acceleration \(\partial_t \mathbf{u}\) of a small fluid parcel with density \( ho\), including buoyancy and the Lorentz force, is:

\[ ho\partial_t \mathbf{u} +2 ho\,\mathbf{\Omega} imes\mathbf{u}=- abla p + rac{1}{\mu_0}( abla imes \mathbf{B}) imes \mathbf{B} + ho\mathbf{g}+ ho u abla^2{\mathbf{u}}, \]

where \(p\) is the reduced pressure, \(\mathbf{B}\) the magnetic field, and \( u\) is the kinematic viscosity of the fluid. Assume small density perturbations \( ho'\) following

\[ ho= ho_0+ ho'= ho_0- ho_0\alpha heta, \]

where \(\alpha\) is the fluid's thermal expansion coefficient and \( heta\) is the temperature variation from the isentropic temperature profile \(T(r)\). Assume also a gravitational acceleration following

\[ \mathbf{g}=-g_0 rac{r}{R}\mathbf{\hat r}. \]

Within the Boussinesq approximation the density variations enter only through the buoyancy force, so

\[ ho\mathbf{g} \longrightarrow ho' \mathbf{g} = ho_0 \alpha g_0 rac{r}{R} heta \mathbf{\hat r}. \]

Now we make the dimensional units explicit. With \(L\) being the unit of length, \( au\) the unit of time, \( heta^*\) the unit of temperature, \(P^*\) the unit of pressure, and \(\mathbf{\hat z}\) the unit vector along \(\mathbf{\Omega}\), then the momentum equation, after dividing by \( ho_0\), is

\[ rac{L}{ au^2}\,\partial_t \mathbf{u} +L rac{\Omega}{ au}\, 2\mathbf{\hat z} imes\mathbf{u}=- rac{P^*}{ ho_0 L} abla p + rac{B_0^2}{L ho_0 \mu_0}( abla imes \mathbf{B}) imes \mathbf{B} + rac{\alpha g_0 heta^*}{R} L r heta\mathbf{\hat r}+ rac{ u }{ au L} abla^2 \mathbf{u}, \]

where it is understood that the variables \(r, t, \mathbf{u}, p, heta, \mathbf{B}\) are now dimensionless. Multiply the equation by \( au^2/L\) and get

\[ \partial_t \mathbf{u} + 2\,\Omega au\,\mathbf{\hat z} imes\mathbf{u}=- abla p + rac{ au^2 B_0^2}{L^2 ho_0 \mu_0}( abla imes \mathbf{B}) imes \mathbf{B} + au^2 rac{\alpha g_0 heta^*}{R} r heta \mathbf{\hat r}+ au rac{ u}{L^2} abla^2 \mathbf{u}. \]

Above we have chosen the pressure scale as \(P^*= ho_0 L^2/ au^2\). For the time being we leave the temperature scale \( heta^*\) unspecified, and define the Ekman number \(E\) as

\[ E \equiv rac{ u}{\Omega L^2}, \]

The Lehnert number \(Le\) as

\[ Le \equiv rac{B_0}{\Omega L \sqrt{ ho_0\mu_0}}, \]

the Rayleigh number \(Ra\) as

\[ Ra \equiv rac{\alpha g_0 heta^* L^4}{ u\kappa R}, \]

and the Prandtl number \(Pr\) as

\[ Pr \equiv rac{ u}{\kappa}, \]

where \(\kappa\) is the thermal diffusivity of the fluid So, the momentum equation becomes

\[ \partial_t \mathbf{u} + 2\,(\Omega au)\,\mathbf{\hat z} imes\mathbf{u}=- abla p + (\Omega au)^2 Le^2( abla imes \mathbf{B}) imes \mathbf{B} + (\Omega au)^2 E^2 rac{Ra}{Pr}\, heta\, r\, \mathbf{\hat r}+(\Omega au)\,E\, abla^2 \mathbf{u}. \]

Alternatively, if we deal with problems without viscosity or thermal diffusion where the Rayleigh number diverges, it is better to define a reference Brunt-Väisälä frequency \(N_0\) such that

\[ N_0^2 \equiv - rac{\alpha g_0 heta^*}{R}. \]

If the Rayleigh number is finite then we can write

\[ E^2 rac{Ra}{Pr} = - rac{N_0^2}{\Omega^2}. \]

The momentum equation, using the reference Brunt-Väisälä frequency reads

\[ \partial_t \mathbf{u} + 2\,(\Omega au)\,\mathbf{\hat z} imes\mathbf{u}=- abla p + (\Omega au)^2 Le^2( abla imes \mathbf{B}) imes \mathbf{B} - (\Omega au)^2 rac{N_0^2}{\Omega^2}\, heta\, r\, \mathbf{\hat r}+(\Omega au)\,E\, abla^2 \mathbf{u}. \]

A common choice for the time scale is the rotation time scale, so \( au=1/\Omega\) and the \((\Omega au)\) factors go away. Another choice is the viscous diffusion time scale, with \( au=L^2/ u\), in which case \(\Omega au=1/E\). Yet another choice is the Alfvén wave time scale, with \( au=L \sqrt{\mu_0 ho_0}/B_0\) so that \(\Omega au=1/Le\).

docs.title: The induction equation
docs.text:
The induction equation in dimensional form is

\[ \partial_t \mathbf{B} = abla imes (\mathbf{u} imes \mathbf{B}) + \eta abla^2 \mathbf{B}, \]

where \(\eta\) is the magnetic diffusivity. Making the dimensional scale factors explicit we get

\[ rac{B_0}{ au} \partial_t \mathbf{B} = rac{B_0}{ au} abla imes (\mathbf{u} imes \mathbf{B}) + \eta rac{B_0}{L^2} abla^2\mathbf{B}, \]

where \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{B}, t\) are now dimensionless. Multiply now by \( au/B_0\) and obtain

\[ \partial_t \mathbf{B} = abla imes (\mathbf{u} imes \mathbf{B}) + (\Omega au)E_\eta abla^2 \mathbf{B}, \]

where \(E_\eta\) is the magnetic Ekman number defined as

\[ E_\eta \equiv rac{\eta}{\Omega L^2}. \]

docs.title: The heat equation
docs.text:
The heat equation in its dimensional form is

\[ \partial_t heta=-\mathbf{u}\cdot abla T+\kappa abla^2 heta. \]

We assume that an isentropic temperature background \(T(r)\) exists, which is only a function of radius. Its gradient is then \( abla T=\mathbf{\hat r}\,\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}r\). Now we write \(\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}r=C\,f(r)\), where \(C\) is a scale factor for the gradient (can be negative) and \(f(r)\) is a dimensionless function of \(r\) (with \(r\) also dimensionless). Then we can write the heat equation, using this time dimensionless variables exclusively as

\[ \partial_t heta=- rac{LC}{ heta^*}\,u_r\,f(r)+(\Omega au) rac{E}{Pr} abla^2 heta. \]

In kore we choose always the temperature scale as \( heta^*=-LC\) so that the heat equation reads simply

\[ \partial_t heta=u_r\,f(r)+(\Omega au) rac{E}{Pr} abla^2 heta. \]

A temperature profile with a linear gradient is common in the literature. In that case \(\partial_r T=- eta r\) (dimensional). In dimensionless variables this is \(- eta L r\) (\(r\) now dimensionless), so that the temperature scale is \( heta^*= eta L^2\). And if the length scale is the CMB radius, i.e. \(L=R\), then the Rayleigh number becomes

\[ Ra = rac{\alpha g_0 eta R^5}{ u\kappa}. \]

docs.title: The composition equation
docs.text:
The composition \(\xi\) is treated like the temperature, with the compositional diffusivity \(D\) in place of \(\kappa\) and a background gradient \(\mathrm{d}C/\mathrm{d}r\) (comp_background). With the composition scale chosen in the same way, the dimensionless equation is

\[ \partial_t \xi = u_r\, f_\xi(r) + (\Omega\tau)\frac{E}{Sc} \nabla^2 \xi, \]

where \(Sc = \nu/D\) is the Schmidt number. Composition adds a buoyancy term \(-(\Omega\tau)^2 \frac{N_\xi^2}{\Omega^2}\,\xi\, r\, \mathbf{\hat r}\) to the momentum equation, with \(N_\xi^2/\Omega^2 = -E^2 Ra_\xi/Sc\) (BV2_comp) and \(Ra_\xi\) the compositional Rayleigh number (Ra_comp).

docs.title: Induction in a conducting inner core
docs.text:
In a solid, conducting inner core there is no flow, and the field there, \(\mathbf{b}_i\), only diffuses:

\[ \partial_t \mathbf{b}_i = (\Omega\tau)\, \frac{E_\eta}{\mu_{i2o}\,\sigma_{i2o}}\, \nabla^2 \mathbf{b}_i, \]

where \(\sigma_{i2o}\) and \(\mu_{i2o}\) are the conductivity and permeability of the inner core relative to the fluid. The conditions that join \(\mathbf{b}_i\) to the field in the fluid are on Inner core and mantle.

docs.title: The equations Kore solves
docs.text:
Collecting the above, the dimensionless equations are

\[ \lambda\,\mathbf{u} = - 2\,(\Omega au)\,\mathbf{\hat z} imes\mathbf{u} - abla p + (\Omega au)^2 Le^2 \left[ ( abla imes\mathbf{b}) imes\mathbf{B}_0 + ( abla imes\mathbf{B}_0) imes\mathbf{b} ight] - (\Omega au)^2 \left( rac{N_0^2}{\Omega^2}\, heta + rac{N_\xi^2}{\Omega^2}\,\xi ight) r\,\mathbf{\hat r} + (\Omega au)\,E\, abla^2\mathbf{u}, \] \[ \lambda\,\mathbf{b} = abla imes(\mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}_0) + (\Omega au)\,E_\eta\, abla^2\mathbf{b}, \] \[ \lambda\, heta = u_r\, f(r) + (\Omega au)\, rac{E}{Pr}\, abla^2 heta, \qquad \lambda\,\xi = u_r\, f_\xi(r) + (\Omega au)\, rac{E}{Sc}\, abla^2\xi, \]

with \( abla\cdot\mathbf{u} = abla\cdot\mathbf{b} = 0\), plus forcing terms in forced problems. The Coriolis term is left out with rotation = 0. With rotdyn = 1 three more equations describe the rotation of the mantle and the inner core (see Rotational dynamics). The parameters map to Kore's names as follows:

Symbol Parameter Definition \(\Omega au\) OmgTau Set by timescale (see Setting up a problem) \(E\) Ek \( u/\Omega L^2\) \(E_\eta\) Em \(\eta/\Omega L^2\) \(Le\) Le (Le2 = \(Le^2\)) \(B_0/\Omega L\sqrt{ ho\mu_0}\) \(\Lambda\), \(Pm\) Lambda, Pm \(Le^2/E_\eta\) and \(E/E_\eta\) \(N_0^2/\Omega^2\) BV2 \(-E^2 Ra/Pr\) \(N_\xi^2/\Omega^2\) BV2_comp \(-E^2 Ra_\xi/Sc\) \(Pr\), \(Sc\) Prandtl, Schmidt \( u/\kappa\), \( u/D\)

The boundary conditions are described in Setting up a problem (flow, temperature, composition) and Inner core and mantle (magnetic field).

docs.title: Angular momentum balance
docs.text: For an axisymmetric, equatorially symmetric problem (\(m = 0\), symm = 1) the fluid, the mantle and the inner core exchange axial angular momentum through the viscous and electromagnetic stresses on the boundaries. Everything below is dimensionless, with angular momentum in units of \(\rho L^5/\tau\) and torques in units of \(\rho L^5/\tau^2\), and everything is a complex amplitude of \(e^{\lambda t}\): the balances are linear, so no complex conjugates are added.

docs.title: The fluid
docs.text:
Only the axisymmetric toroidal flow of degree 1, \(u_\phi = t_1(r)\sin heta\), carries axial angular momentum:

\[ L_z = \int s\, u_\phi\, dV = rac{8\pi}{3} \int_{r_i}^{1} r^3\, t_1(r)\, dr , \]

with \(s = r\sin heta\) the distance to the axis. Its rate of change is the total axial torque on the fluid. The Coriolis force and the pressure exert no axial torque on the fluid as a whole, and the torque of the Lorentz force reduces to the Maxwell stress on the boundaries, so the fluid only exchanges angular momentum with the mantle and the inner core:

\[ \lambda\, L_z = - \left( \Gamma^{ u}_M + \Gamma^{B}_M + \Gamma^{ u}_{IC} + \Gamma^{B}_{IC} ight), \]

where \(\Gamma^{ u}\) and \(\Gamma^{B}\) are the viscous and electromagnetic torques that the fluid exerts on the mantle (\(M\)) and on the inner core (\(IC\)). This is the balance that spin_doctor's resid𝐋 checks, and it holds whether or not the boundaries are free to rotate.

docs.title: The torques
docs.text:
The viscous torque is the surface integral of the azimuthal viscous stress \(\sigma_{r\phi} = r\,\partial_r (u_\phi/r)\), which for the degree-1 flow depends on \(t_1\) at the boundary only:

\[ \Gamma^{\nu}_M = -\,E\,(\Omega\tau) \oint_{CMB} s\, \sigma_{r\phi}\, dS = -\frac{8\pi}{3}\, E\,(\Omega\tau)\, \left( r\, t_1' - t_1 \right)_{r = 1}, \] \[ \Gamma^{\nu}_{IC} = +\,E\,(\Omega\tau) \oint_{ICB} s\, \sigma_{r\phi}\, dS = \frac{8\pi}{3}\, E\,(\Omega\tau)\, r_i^2 \left( r\, t_1' - t_1 \right)_{r = r_i} . \]

The electromagnetic torque is the surface integral of the Maxwell stress \(B_{0r}\, b_\phi\) (the background field is poloidal, so \(B_{0\phi} = 0\)):

\[ \Gamma^{B}_M = -\,Le^2 (\Omega\tau)^2 \oint_{CMB} s\, B_{0r}\, b_\phi\, dS, \qquad \Gamma^{B}_{IC} = +\,Le^2 (\Omega\tau)^2 \oint_{ICB} s\, B_{0r}\, b_\phi\, dS . \]

It is nonzero only on a body in which currents can flow: the mantle with a thin conducting wall, the inner core when it is conducting or has a thin wall. Since \(B_{0r} \propto Y_l^0\) and \(b_\phi\) comes from the toroidal scalars of \(\mathbf{b}\), the integral selects a few toroidal degrees: \(g_2\) at the boundary for a degree-1 background field ('axial', the dipoles, FDM with B0_l = 1), and \(g_1\) and \(g_3\) for the quadrupole 'Luo_S2'. spin_doctor writes these four torques, as complex amplitudes, to flow.dat and magnetic.dat.

docs.title: The mantle and the inner core
docs.text:
With rotdyn = 0 the mantle and the inner core rotate with the frame, and the torques above are simply what the fluid exerts on them. With rotdyn = 1 they respond to those torques, to the gravitational torque between them, and to the viscous relaxation of the inner core (see Rotational dynamics):

\[ \lambda\, I_M\, \omega_M = \Gamma^{\nu}_M + \Gamma^{B}_M + K \varphi, \] \[ \lambda\, I_{IC}\, \omega_{IC} = \Gamma^{\nu}_{IC} + \Gamma^{B}_{IC} - K \varphi, \] \[ \lambda\, \varphi = \omega_{IC} - \omega_M - \frac{\Omega\tau}{\Omega\tau_{IC}}\, \varphi , \]

with \(I_M\) and \(I_{IC}\) the axial moments of inertia (MoIZ_M, MoIZ_IC, in units of \(\rho L^5\)), \(\omega_M\) and \(\omega_{IC}\) the rotation rates relative to the frame, \(\varphi\) the longitude of the inner core relative to the mantle, \(K\) = gTorque\(\,(\Omega\tau)^2\) the gravitational coupling constant and \(\Omega\tau_{IC}\) = OmgtauIC. The solid bodies enter the fluid's equations through the no-slip condition on \(t_1\): \(t_1(1) = \omega_M\) and \(t_1(r_i) = r_i\,\omega_{IC}\) instead of zero.

docs.title: Conservation
docs.text:
Adding the three balances, the gravitational torque cancels (it is internal to the mantle-inner core system) and the boundary torques cancel against the fluid's, so the total axial angular momentum is conserved:

\[ \lambda \left( L_z + I_M\, \omega_M + I_{IC}\, \omega_{IC} \right) = 0 . \]

For a mode with \(\lambda \neq 0\) the total must therefore vanish, and Kore's eigenmodes satisfy this to discretisation error (about \(10^{-4}\) at \(N = 48\), improving with resolution). With rotdyn = 0 the mantle and the inner core are infinitely heavy, and the fluid's angular momentum alone decays or oscillates at the rate set by the torques.

docs.title: Examples and tests
docs.text: The test cases in tests/ reproduce published results and serve as worked examples. Each folder holds a complete parameter file, which can be copied to bin/parameters.py of a run folder to run the case by hand.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
cd tests
pytest . -v -s

Each test copies bin/ into its case folder, installs the case's parameter file as bin/parameters.py, runs Kore there with 2 MPI processes, compares the result with the reference and cleans up. All the tests together take a few minutes. They also run on GitHub Actions at every push to the conductive_IC branch, with the Ubuntu PETSc and SLEPc packages (complex scalars). Without pytest, the test methods can be called directly from python.

docs.title: The default torsional mode
docs.text: The parameters in bin/parameters.py set up a torsional Alfvén mode: an \(l = 1\) free-decay-mode field, \(\Lambda = 10\), \(Pm = 0.1\), \(E = 10^{-7}\), ricb = 0.35, no-slip boundaries, an insulating inner core and a thin conducting wall at the CMB (c_cmb = 0.01, c1_cmb = 0.015). The mode closest to the target is \(\lambda = -0.00464013 + 0.01150398\,i\) in rotation units, with Tor/Pol = 156 and Mag/Kin = 1.01. The Quick start runs it step by step.

docs.title: Spin-over mode
docs.text:
tests/spinover, run by test_spinover.py. A hydrodynamic problem: \(m = 1\), antisymmetric, \(E = 10^{-3}\), ricb = 0.35, no-slip boundaries, \(N = 68\), \(l_{max} = 64\), without pre-scaling. The least damped of the 5 eigenvalues found around the default target (\(i\)) is the spin-over mode,

\[ \lambda = -0.1019947097 + 1.0057336901\,i, \]

which must be matched to \(10^{-8}\).

docs.title: Torsional modes of a quadrupolar field
docs.text:
tests/torsional_s2, run by test_torsional_s2.py. The first two torsional modes of the quadrupolar background field S2 of Luo & Jackson (2022, Proc. R. Soc. A 478, 20210982, table 1): an inviscid full sphere (Ek = 0, ricb = 0), insulating boundary, \(Le = 10^{-4}\), Lundquist number \(2\times10^4\), Alfvén time scale, cnorm = 'mag_energy', \(N = 128\), \(l_{max} = 127\):

par.ricb      = 0
par.Ek        = 0
par.magnetic  = 1
par.B0        = 'Luo_S2'
par.cnorm     = 'mag_energy'  # unit magnetic energy as in Luo & Jackson 2022
Lu            = 2e4
par.Le        = 1e-4
par.Em        = par.Le/Lu
par.timescale = 'Alfven'
par.N         = 128           # set manually (Ncheb is for viscous runs)
par.rtau      = -0.0142       # mode 2
par.itau      = 1.9095

The matrices are built once and solved twice, around each mode, since a mode far from the target is less accurate. Mode 1 uses a target given on the command line:

mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/solve_nopp.py -eps_target -0.0066+1.0336i
Mode Kore (\(N = 128\)) Luo & Jackson (2022) 1 \(-0.0065950164 + 1.0335952716\,i\) \(-0.0065952461 + 1.0335959942\,i\) 2 \(-0.0141843686 + 1.9095212618\,i\) \(-0.0141833345 + 1.9095123626\,i\)

The test requires Kore's values to \(10^{-7}\) and the published ones to \(2\times10^{-6}\) (mode 1) and \(10^{-5}\) (mode 2), relative to \(|\lambda|\).

docs.title: Onset of convection
docs.text:
test_convection_bouss.py finds the critical Rayleigh number at which the least stable mode stops decaying, with tests/find_Rac.py: a root search on the growth rate as a function of the Rayleigh number based on the gap width, Ra_gap = Ra\(\,(1 - r_i)^3\). Both cases use \(Pr = 1\), \(m = 9\), no-slip boundaries, which_eigenpairs = 'TR' with a target on the real axis, and -eps_balance twoside.

Case Setup \(Ra_c\) (gap) Drift frequency \(\omega_c\) Jones, Soward & Mussa (2000), tests/jones2000 Full sphere, internal heating, fixed heat flux, \(Ta = 10^9\) (\(E = 6.325\times10^{-5}\)), \(N = 118\) \(4.66986\times10^{6}\) \(-1.93444\times10^{-2}\) Dormy et al. (2004), tests/dormy2004 ricb = 0.35, differential heating, fixed temperatures, \(E = 2\times10^{-5}\), \(N = 74\), g = 2 \(1.65404\times10^{6}\) \(-1.10162\times10^{-2}\)

find_Rac.py can also be run by hand from a case folder that has bin/ with the case's parameter file: ../find_Rac.py Ramin m [ncpus]. The parameter file must contain a line Ra_gap = ..., which the script rewrites before each solve.

docs.title: Thermo-compositional convection
docs.text: tests/silva2019, run by test_thermocompositional.py. With equal Prandtl and Schmidt numbers, temperature and composition combine into a single co-density, and the onset of convection depends only on the sum of the thermal and compositional Rayleigh numbers (Silva, Mather & Simitev 2019, GAFD, eq. 18): with \(R_t = Ra\cos\alpha\) and \(R_c = Ra\sin\alpha\), \(Ra_c(\alpha)\,(\cos\alpha + \sin\alpha)\) is the same for every \(\alpha\). The test finds \(Ra_c\) for \(\alpha\) = 0 (temperature only), \(\pi/2\) (composition only) and \(\pi/4\) (both), with \(Pr = Sc = 1\), Coriolis number \(10^4\), ricb = 0.35, \(m = 7\), stress-free boundaries and fixed temperature and composition, and checks that this sum and the drift frequency agree to \(5\times10^{-5}\).

docs.title: No rotation
docs.text: tests/norotation, run by test_norotation.py. With rotation = 0 and the viscous time scale, the toroidal flow in a full sphere decays freely, with eigenvalues \(\lambda = -k^2\), where \(k\) is the smallest root of \(j_l(k) = 0\) for a no-slip boundary or of \(k\,j_l'(k) = j_l(k)\) for a stress-free one. The test checks \(l\) = 2 and 3, both boundary conditions and \(m\) = 0, 1 and 2, to \(10^{-10}\); the decay rate must not depend on \(m\).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To run kore we need the PETSc/SLEPc packages and their python bindings petsc4py/slepc4py. PETSc needs to be compiled with support for complex scalars. MUMPS and SuperLU_dist are external packages that need to be installed together with PETSc.

If you are interested in problems that involve very large matrices, for instance when considering extremely small viscosities, we recommend doing so with a machine with at least 128 GB of memory. The number of processing cores is not critical, eight are fine, 24 are plenty. Small to moderate size matrices can be solved using a laptop, depending on available memory.

docs.title: Installing PETSc/SLEPc on MacOS
docs.text:
It is convenient to have a dedicated python environment to use with kore. It is quite simple to create and activate it:

python3 -m venv kore_env
source kore_env/bin/activate

Then we need to install scipy and cython in that environment: 

pip3 install scipy cython

Now we download the latest PETSc/SLEPc releases using git 

git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/petsc/petsc.git petsc
git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/slepc/slepc slepc

We go now into the newly created petsc folder and configure PETSc: 

cd petsc
./configure --with-petsc4py --download-mpi4py --download-mpich --with-scalar-type=complex --download-mumps --download-parmetis --download-metis --download-scalapack --download-openblas --download-openblas-make-options='USE_THREAD=0 USE_OPENMP=0 USE_LOCKING=1' --with-debugging=0 --download-superlu_dist --download-ptscotch CXXOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' FOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' COPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' --download-bison
We recommend OpenBLAS (--download-openblas) rather than the reference BLAS/LAPACK (--download-fblaslapack). MUMPS spends most of its factorization time in dense BLAS kernels, and with OpenBLAS the LU factorization was 5 to 8 times faster in our tests (Linux, 24-core Threadripper, MUMPS 5.8.2). For example, a torsional-mode run at N = 976 took 4.4 minutes instead of 20. The make options build a single-threaded OpenBLAS, so that it doesn't compete with the MPI processes for cores.

Then we build PETSc: 

make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt all
where you must replace /path/to/petsc with the actual path for your case. Before checking that everything works we must tell python where to find petsc4py and mpi4py, which were compiled along in the step above: 
export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/petsc/arch-darwin-c-opt/lib
where again we must replace /path/to/petsc with the actual path. Now we test the installation: 
make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt check
If no errors appear then you can proceed to install SLEPc. If an error is reported due to python not being able to find PETSc (even though we just updated the PYTHONPATH), but the other MPI tests were successful, then don't worry, it is safe to ignore the error.

We need to setup some environment variables before installing SLEPc: 

export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc

Now go to the slepc folder, configure and build SLEPc: 

cd $SLEPC_DIR
./configure
make
make check
The last step is to install slepc4py, which is distributed along with SLEPc: 
cd $SLEPC_DIR/src/binding/slepc4py
python3 setup.py build
python3 setup.py install
Almost there now. We need to update the PATH environment variable so that we can use the MPI library provided by PETSc instead of the one provided by your system, if any: 
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH

It is a good idea to keep the necessary commands for initialization in a separate file. It should contain the following lines: 

source /path/to/kore_env/bin/activate
export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-darwin-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc
export PYTHONPATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH
We can write that to a file named e.g. kore_env.sh in your home directory, so every time you need to prepare to run kore we do first: 
source $HOME/kore_env.sh

docs.title: Installing PETSc/SLEPc on Linux
docs.text:
The steps are the same as for MacOS, except for the name of the PETSc architecture (arch-linux-c-opt) and the way slepc4py is built. These instructions were tested on Debian 13 with gcc/gfortran 14 and PETSc/SLEPc 3.25.

First we need compilers and a few build tools. On Debian or Ubuntu they can be installed with: 

sudo apt install build-essential gfortran git cmake python3-dev python3-venv

Then we create and activate a dedicated python environment for kore, and install scipy and cython in it: 

python3 -m venv kore_env
source kore_env/bin/activate
pip3 install scipy cython

Now we download the latest PETSc/SLEPc releases using git 

git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/petsc/petsc.git petsc
git clone -b release https://gitlab.com/slepc/slepc slepc

We go now into the newly created petsc folder and configure PETSc, using OpenBLAS as explained in the MacOS section: 

cd petsc
./configure --with-petsc4py --download-mpi4py --download-mpich --with-scalar-type=complex --download-mumps --download-parmetis --download-metis --download-scalapack --download-openblas --download-openblas-make-options='USE_THREAD=0 USE_OPENMP=0 USE_LOCKING=1' --with-debugging=0 --download-superlu_dist --download-ptscotch CXXOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' FOPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' COPTFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' --download-bison
Then we build PETSc: 
make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt all
where you must replace /path/to/petsc with the actual path for your case. Before checking that everything works we must tell python where to find petsc4py and mpi4py, which were compiled along in the step above: 
export PYTHONPATH=/path/to/petsc/arch-linux-c-opt/lib
Now we test the installation: 
make PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt check

We need to setup some environment variables before installing SLEPc: 

export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH

Now go to the slepc folder, configure and build SLEPc. The --with-slepc4py option builds slepc4py along with SLEPc, inside $SLEPC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib: 

cd $SLEPC_DIR
./configure --with-slepc4py
make
make check

As for MacOS, it is a good idea to keep the necessary commands for initialization in a separate file. Note that PYTHONPATH must now include the SLEPc folder too, so that python finds slepc4py: 

source /path/to/kore_env/bin/activate
export PETSC_DIR=/path/to/petsc
export PETSC_ARCH=arch-linux-c-opt
export SLEPC_DIR=/path/to/slepc
export PYTHONPATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib:$SLEPC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/lib
export PATH=$PETSC_DIR/$PETSC_ARCH/bin:$PATH
We can write that to e.g. $HOME/kore_env.sh and do source $HOME/kore_env.sh before running kore.

Several PETSc builds can live side by side in the same petsc and slepc folders, each under its own PETSC_ARCH name (passed as PETSC_ARCH=... to PETSc's ./configure). Switching between them only requires changing PETSC_ARCH.

docs.title: Optional: SHTns and pyevtk
docs.text:
Kore itself needs neither. The plotting package koreviz (see Output and postprocessing) uses SHTns, a fast spherical-harmonic transform library, to evaluate solutions on a grid in physical space, and koreviz.writeVts uses pyevtk to write files for ParaView.

The script tools/install-shtns.sh downloads SHTns 3.5.2, builds it with OpenMP (with MKL if MKLROOT is set, otherwise with FFTW, which must then be installed) and installs it under $HOME/.local, together with its python module. pyevtk can be installed with pip3 install pyevtk in the Kore python environment.

docs.title: Numerical method
docs.text: This page gives an overview of how Kore turns the equations into matrices. It is not needed to run the code, but it helps when reading the source or the solution files.

docs.title: Unknowns
docs.text:
The flow and the magnetic field are written in poloidal-toroidal form and expanded in spherical harmonics \(Y_l^m\). For one azimuthal wave number \(m\),

\[ \mathbf{u} = \sum_l abla imes abla imes\left( P_l(r)\, Y_l^m\, \mathbf{r} ight) + abla imes\left( T_l(r)\, Y_l^m\, \mathbf{r} ight), \qquad \mathbf{b} = \sum_l abla imes abla imes\left( f_l(r)\, Y_l^m\, \mathbf{r} ight) + abla imes\left( g_l(r)\, Y_l^m\, \mathbf{r} ight), \]

and the temperature and composition are expanded directly in \(Y_l^m\). Because the problem is linear and axisymmetric, different \(m\) do not couple, and the two equatorial symmetries separate: each one keeps every other degree \(l\) in the poloidal part and the remaining ones in the toroidal part. So each of the poloidal and toroidal parts has \((l_{max} - m + 1)/2\) degrees.

In radius, each scalar is expanded in Chebyshev polynomials on \([r_i, 1]\), N of them with an inner core. In a full sphere (ricb = 0) each scalar has a definite parity in \(r\), so only the even or the odd polynomials are used: N/2 coefficients.

The unknown vector holds, in this order: the flow (\(P\), then \(T\)), the magnetic field (\(f\), then \(g\)), the 3 rotational unknowns (\(\omega_M\), \(\omega_{IC}\), \(\varphi\)) with rotdyn = 1, the inner-core field (\(f_i\), then \(g_i\), N_cic/2 coefficients per degree) with a conducting inner core, the temperature and the composition. Within each part the coefficients are grouped by degree \(l\). This is also the layout of the .field files.

docs.title: Sparse spectral method
docs.text:
Each equation is projected so that it involves only the scalars: the radial component of the curl of the curl of the momentum equation for \(P\), the radial component of its curl for \(T\), and the corresponding projections of the induction equation for \(f\) and \(g\). The equations are multiplied by a suitable power of \(r\) so that all their coefficients are polynomials in \(r\).

Kore then uses the ultraspherical spectral method (Olver & Townsend 2013). A derivative of order \(k\) maps Chebyshev polynomials to Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) polynomials \(C^{(k)}\) with a sparse matrix, multiplication by a polynomial is banded in the Gegenbauer basis, and conversions between bases are banded too. An equation of order \(k\) is therefore represented by a sparse, banded matrix in the \(C^{(k)}\) basis, instead of the dense matrix of a collocation method. The boundary conditions replace the first rows of each block (a tau method).

The work is split in three programs:

  1. submatrices.py builds the radial operators (each combination of a power of \(r\), a radial profile and a derivative) and writes them as *.mtx files.
  2. assemble.py combines them into the matrices \(A\) and \(B\), block by block in \(l\), adding the coupling between neighbouring degrees (Coriolis, Lorentz and induction terms), the boundary conditions and, if needed, the inner-core and rotational blocks. The degrees are distributed over the MPI processes in equal blocks, which is why lmax - m + 1 must be divisible by 2*ncpus.
  3. solve_nopp.py solves \(A\,x = \lambda B\,x\) by shift-and-invert around the target, with a sparse LU factorisation of \(A - \tau B\) by MUMPS (see Solver settings), or \(A\,x = b\) for a forced problem.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
solve_nopp.py writes the solutions to the run folder:

File Content eigenvalues0.dat Eigenvalue problems: one row per solution, damping \(\sigma\) and frequency \(\omega\) (\(\lambda = \sigma + i\omega\)). real_flow.field, imag_flow.field Real and imaginary parts of the flow's spectral coefficients, one column per solution. real_magnetic.field, imag_magnetic.field The magnetic field perturbation, with magnetic = 1. real_magnetic_ic.field, imag_magnetic_ic.field The field inside a conducting inner core ('conducting, Chebys'). real_temperature.field, real_composition.field (and imag_) Temperature and composition, when included. rotdyn.field Mantle and inner-core rotation rates and their angle, as complex numbers, with rotdyn = 1. timing.dat Total run time of solve_nopp.py, in seconds. no_conv_solution Written instead when no eigenvalue converged.

The coefficients are ordered by spherical-harmonic degree, poloidal part first and then toroidal, with the Chebyshev coefficients of each degree together (see Numerical method). tools/load_solution.py loads a solution into an interactive python session.

Eigenvectors are only defined up to a complex factor. Kore scales each one so that its kinetic plus magnetic energy in the fluid equals 1 (see Solver settings); its phase is arbitrary. Forced solutions keep the amplitude set by the forcing.

docs.title: spin_doctor
docs.text:
./bin/spin_doctor.py ncpus

spin_doctor.py computes, for every solution in the folder, the energies, dissipation rates, work of the forces and torques, and residuals of the energy and angular-momentum balances that show how accurate the solution is. It prints a summary table and appends the results to the .dat files below. It needs the flow (hydro = 1).

docs.title: The summary table
docs.text:
Column Meaning ★ Solution number. Damping σ, Frequency ω Real and imaginary parts of the eigenvalue (the forcing frequency for forced problems). resid0, resid𝐮, resid𝐛, residθ, resid𝐋 Residuals of the balances, see below. Tor/Pol Toroidal over poloidal kinetic energy. Mag/Kin Magnetic over kinetic energy. Geo Geostrophic fraction: the share of the energy of \(u_\phi\) held by its average along the rotation axis (see below). Only for \(m = 0\), symm = 1; nan otherwise. |𝚪|mag Modulus of the electromagnetic torque on the mantle. |𝚪|magIC Modulus of the electromagnetic torque on the inner core.

The geostrophic fraction measures how close the azimuthal flow is to being invariant along the rotation axis:

\[ \text{Geo} = \frac{\int |\langle u_\phi \rangle|^2\,dV}{\int |u_\phi|^2\,dV}, \qquad \langle u_\phi \rangle(s) = \frac{1}{H}\int u_\phi\,dz , \]

where the average is taken along each fluid column of height \(H\), from the inner core (or the equator, outside the tangent cylinder) to the core-mantle boundary. Since the column average and the rest of \(u_\phi\) are orthogonal, \(1 - \text{Geo}\) is the share of the energy of \(u_\phi\) in its \(z\)-dependent part. A torsional mode has Geo close to 1 (with Tor/Pol \(\gg 1\) and Mag/Kin \(\approx 1\)); in the inviscid full sphere it is 1 to round-off. It is computed by geostrophic_fraction in bin/utils4pp.py, on a grid of 240 cells in \(s\) and 48 Gauss-Legendre points in \(z\) over the northern half of the fluid (\(u_\phi\) is equatorially symmetric for \(m = 0\), symm = 1). These points do not resolve the Ekman layers, so Geo describes the interior flow.

docs.title: Checking the results
docs.text:
The residuals compare terms of balances that an exact solution satisfies. They are computed from the solution alone, independently of the solver, and are the best test of a solution's accuracy. Each is the size of the imbalance divided by the largest term:

Residual Balance resid0 The viscous dissipation computed in two ways, from \(\int \mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla^2\mathbf{u}\,dV\) and from the rate of strain. nan if Ek = 0. resid𝐮 Kinetic energy: \(2\sigma\) times the kinetic energy against the viscous dissipation and the work of the Lorentz and buoyancy forces. resid𝐛 Magnetic energy: \(2\sigma\) times the magnetic energy against the induction work and magnetic diffusion. residθ Thermal "energy": \(2\sigma\) times it against thermal diffusion and advection. resid𝐋 Axial angular momentum of the fluid: \(\lambda L_z\) against the viscous and electromagnetic torques on the mantle and the inner core (see Angular momentum balance). Only for eigenvalue problems with \(m = 0\), symm = 1; nan otherwise.

As a rule of thumb they should all be below about \(10^{-4}\). If they are not, increase the resolution. Exceptions and caveats:

  • With rotdyn = 1, resid0 stays at about \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-3}\), because the work done by the rotating mantle and inner core on the fluid is not included in that balance yet.
  • The eigenvectors of the modes found away from the target are usually less accurate than the one closest to \(\tau\). To get a particular mode as accurately as possible, place the target on it.
  • The residuals do not detect a too small lmax. Keep lmax close to N (see Solver settings).
  • The energy balances cover the fluid only. Ohmic losses in a conducting inner core or a thin wall enter only through the flux of magnetic energy across the boundary, which \(\int \mathbf{b}\cdot\nabla^2\mathbf{b}\,dV\) contains implicitly.
  • With Ek = 0 and an insulating mantle there are no torques, and resid𝐋 is 1 by construction.
  • solve_nopp.py also prints a residual for each eigenvalue, \(\|Ax-\lambda Bx\|/\|\lambda x\|\). It only shows that SLEPc converged, and stays small even for inaccurate eigenvectors. Judge accuracy by spin_doctor's residuals.

docs.title: Result files
docs.text:
Each run appends one row per solution to the files below, in the same order in every file. Several runs in the same folder therefore build up a table of results, which tools/getresults.py can load.

params.dat, the parameters of the run (58 columns): hydro, magnetic, thermal, compositional, Ek, m, symm, ricb, bci, bco, forcing, forcing_frequency, forcing_amplitude_cmb, forcing_amplitude_icb, projection, B0type, beta_actual, B0_l, innercore_mag_bc, c_icb, c1_icb, mantle_mag_bc, c_cmb, c1_cmb, mu, Em, Le2, B0_norm, Etherm, heating, BV2, rc, h, rsy, bci_thermal, bco_thermal, Ecomp, compositional_background, BV2_comp, rcc, hc, rsyc, bci_compositional, bco_compositional, OmgTau, ncpus, N, lmax, runtime, mu_i2o, sigma_i2o, aux1, aux2, rotdyn, MoIZ_M, MoIZ_IC, OmgtauIC, gTorque. Text options are stored as their position in the list of options: B0type in ['axial', 'dipole', 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1', 'Luo_S2', 'FDM'], innercore_mag_bc in ['insulator', 'TWA', 'conducting, Chebys', 'conducting, Bessel'], mantle_mag_bc in ['insulator', 'TWA'], heating in ['internal', 'differential', 'two zone', 'user defined']. runtime is the total time of solve_nopp.py plus spin_doctor.py.

eigenvalues.dat: damping \(\sigma\) and frequency \(\omega\).

flow.dat (19 columns; 18 in files written before 2026-10-11):

Columns Quantity 1-3 Kinetic energy: total, poloidal, toroidal 4 Viscous dissipation from \(\int \mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla^2\mathbf{u}\,dV\) 5 Viscous (internal) dissipation from the rate of strain 6-8 Work of the Lorentz force, the thermal and the compositional buoyancy 9-10 resid0, resid𝐮 11-12 Viscous torque on the mantle (real, imaginary) 13-14 Viscous torque on the inner core (real, imaginary) 15 Pressure term 16 Unused (0) 17-18 Axial angular momentum of the fluid \(L_z\) (real, imaginary) 19 Geostrophic fraction of \(u_\phi\) (nan unless \(m = 0\), symm = 1)

magnetic.dat (8 columns): magnetic energy, magnetic diffusion, induction work, resid𝐛, electromagnetic torque on the mantle (real, imaginary), electromagnetic torque on the inner core (real, imaginary).

thermal.dat (4 columns): thermal "energy", thermal advection, thermal diffusion, residθ.

compositional.dat (3 columns): compositional "energy", advection, diffusion.

rotdyn.dat (8 complex columns): see Rotational dynamics.

Energies, dissipation rates and work are in the units set by timescale, with the magnetic energy scaled so that kinetic and magnetic energies are comparable (an eigenvector has kinetic plus magnetic energy 1). Torques are the axial torques the fluid exerts on the mantle and the inner core, as complex amplitudes.

docs.text:
Run them from the run folder (they read bin/parameters.py and the .field files there):

docs.title: koreviz
docs.text:
koreviz is a python package for plots and 3D output of a solution. It needs SHTns (see Installation). In python, from the run folder (which contains koreviz/ and bin/):

import koreviz as kv
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

u = kv.kmode(field='u', solnum=0)      # flow of solution 0 on a grid
u.merid(field='uphi')                  # meridional section of u_phi
u.surf(field='ur', r=0.9)              # u_r on the sphere r = 0.9
u.equat(field='ur')                    # equatorial section

b = kv.kmode(field='b', solnum=0, ic=True)   # magnetic field, also inside the inner core
b.merid(field='bphi', ic=True)               # the section continues into the inner core

plt.show()

The field names are ur, utheta, uphi, br, btheta, bphi, temperature, composition, energy (kinetic energy density) and vortz (axial vorticity, with vort=True). With ic=True the field inside the inner core is the computed one for 'conducting, Chebys', and the matching potential field for 'insulator' and 'TWA'. potextra(rout) returns the potential field outside the CMB (or inside an insulating inner core) at the radii rout. kv.writeVts(mode, scals=[...], vecs=[...]) writes out.vts for ParaView (needs pyevtk), optionally with the potential field outside the core (potextra=True).

docs.text:
The scripts in tools/ help with parameter studies on a PBS-managed cluster. Edit the paths in them first (they assume the code in ~/kore and runs in ~/data).

With mode = e the values are powers of ten (\(10^{start}\), ...), with d they are linear. Example: ./dodirs.sh run_Ek_ Ek e -5 -0.1 -6. dosubs.sh (same arguments) Submits the runs, using subramp.sh as the job script. reap.sh prefix Collects the results of all the folders into prefix.par, .flo, .eig, .mag and .thm. getresults.py %run -i tools/getresults.py prefix loads the collected results (or the .dat files of the current folder) in IPython. join.sh label1 label2 out Concatenates two collected data sets.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page runs the case that comes with the code, a torsional Alfvén mode, from start to finish. It assumes PETSc and SLEPc are installed and their environment is loaded (see Installation).

docs.title: Get the code
docs.text:
Clone the repository: 

git clone https://github.com/repepo/kore.git
For regular work, make a copy of the source directory and keep the original clean. For example: 
cp -r kore kwork1
cd kwork1
All the commands below are run from this top folder (kwork1 here). The matrices, solutions and results are written there.

docs.title: Set the parameters
docs.text:
Every parameter, its default value and the available options are defined in bin/params_default.py. The file you edit is bin/parameters.py. It creates the parameter object par, changes only what differs from the defaults, and ends with par.set_scales(), which computes the derived parameters (the magnetic Ekman and Lehnert numbers, the time scale factor, the resolution, the solver target, ...). The version in the repository sets up a torsional-mode problem:

par = default_params()

# Torsional-mode setup: FDM field with a thin conducting wall at the CMB
par.Ek       = 10**-7
par.magnetic = 1
par.B0       = 'FDM'     # torsional waves need B_s != 0, the axial field has none
par.mantle   = 'TWA'
par.c_cmb    = 1e-2
par.c1_cmb   = 1.5e-2    # magnetic torque ~ viscous torque
par.Lambda   = 10        # Le = sqrt(Lambda*Ek/Pm) = 3.2e-3
par.Pm       = 0.1       # Lundquist number Le/Em = 3.2e3

par.rtau     = -0.0046   # aims at the mode lambda = -0.00463 + 0.0115i
par.itau     = 0.0115

par.set_scales()

The other parameters keep their defaults: an inner core of radius 0.35 (the CMB radius is 1), no-slip boundaries, an insulating inner core, \(m = 0\), the rotation time scale, and \(N\) = 232 Chebyshev polynomials with \(l_{max}\) = 231 at this Ekman number. Always set parameters before par.set_scales(): a change made after it does not reach the derived parameters. Setting up a problem describes all the parameters.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
A run has four steps. ncpus is the number of MPI processes. For the first two steps it must equal par.ncpus (4 by default), because the spherical-harmonic degrees are distributed in equal blocks among the processes.

  1. Generate the submatrices, the building blocks of the operators, as *.mtx files: 
    ./bin/submatrices.py ncpus
  2. Assemble the matrices \(A\) and \(B\) of the eigenvalue problem \(A\,x = \lambda B\,x\) (or the matrix and right-hand side of a forced problem), written as A.npz and B.npz: 
    mpiexec -n ncpus ./bin/assemble.py
  3. Solve. The number of processes can differ from par.ncpus here. Solver options can be appended to the command (see Solver settings): 
    mpiexec -n ncpus ./bin/solve_nopp.py
  4. Postprocess: compute energies, dissipation, torques and the residuals that tell whether the solutions are accurate: 
    ./bin/spin_doctor.py ncpus

The script bin/runKore.sh runs the four steps with 4 processes.

Output and postprocessing explains every column, the files that are written and the plotting tools.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text: The solutions are written as real_*.field and imag_*.field (one column per solution) and, for eigenvalue problems, eigenvalues0.dat. spin_doctor.py appends one line per solution to params.dat, eigenvalues.dat, flow.dat, magnetic.dat (with a magnetic field) and, when they are included, thermal.dat, compositional.dat and rotdyn.dat. Because these files are appended to, several runs in the same folder build up a table of results.
