docs.title: Rotational dynamics
docs.text: By default the mantle and the inner core rotate rigidly with the reference frame. With rotdyn = 1 they can instead respond to the axial torques that the fluid exerts on them, and to the gravitational torque between them. The inner core can also relax viscously towards gravitational alignment with the mantle. This couples the fluid's axisymmetric zonal flow (for example torsional modes) to changes in the rotation of the mantle and the inner core.

docs.title: Unknowns and equations
docs.text:
rotdyn = 1 adds three unknowns to the problem: the mantle and inner-core rotation rates relative to the frame, \(\omega_M\) and \(\omega_{IC}\), and the angle between the inner core and the mantle, \(\varphi\). Their equations, for a mode with eigenvalue \(\lambda\), are

\[ \lambda\, I_M\, \omega_M = \Gamma^{ u}_M + \Gamma^{B}_M + K \varphi, \] \[ \lambda\, I_{IC}\, \omega_{IC} = \Gamma^{ u}_{IC} + \Gamma^{B}_{IC} - K \varphi, \] \[ \lambda\, \varphi = \omega_{IC} - \omega_M - rac{\Omega au}{\Omega au_{IC}}\, \varphi . \]

\(I_M\) and \(I_{IC}\) are the axial moments of inertia, \(\Gamma^ u\) and \(\Gamma^B\) the viscous and electromagnetic torques of the fluid on each body, and \(K\) the gravitational coupling constant. The last term in the third equation is the viscous relaxation of the inner core, with relaxation time \( au_{IC}\). The fluid is coupled to the solid bodies through the no-slip condition on the axisymmetric toroidal flow of degree 1: its value at the CMB is \(r_{cmb}\,\omega_M\) and at the ICB \(r_i\,\omega_{IC}\), instead of zero.

The viscous torques scale with \(E\,(\Omega au)\), the electromagnetic torques with \(Le^2 (\Omega au)^2\), and the gravitational one with \((\Omega au)^2\), so all are in the units set by timescale. An electromagnetic torque exists only on a body that conducts: the mantle with mantle = 'TWA', the inner core with 'conducting, Chebys' or 'TWA' (see Inner core and mantle).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning rotdyn 0 1 lets the mantle and the inner core respond to axial torques. MoIZ_M 11.16 Axial moment of inertia of the mantle, \(I_M\), in units of \(\rho L^5\). MoIZ_IC \(9.2\times10^{-3}\) Axial moment of inertia of the inner core, \(I_{IC}\), in units of \(\rho L^5\). gTorque \(5\times10^{-8}\) Gravitational torque constant, divided by \(\rho L^5 \Omega^2\). \(K\) = gTorque * OmgTau**2. OmgtauIC \(2.3\times10^{3}\) \(\Omega\tau_{IC}\), the inner core's viscous relaxation time times the rotation rate. 2300 corresponds to \(\tau_{IC}\) = 1 year for the Earth. vtrq 1 0 switches off the viscous torques on the mantle and the inner core. mtrq 1 0 switches off the electromagnetic torques.

The default moments of inertia and coupling constant are Earth-like values.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• An axisymmetric, equatorially symmetric problem: m = 0, symm = 1.
  • An inner core (ricb > 0) and no-slip boundaries (bci = bco = 1, Ek > 0), since the solid bodies drag the fluid through the no-slip condition.
  • Eigenvalue problems. The rotation of the boundaries in forced problems (libration) is prescribed through forcing instead.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
solve_nopp.py writes the three unknowns of each solution to rotdyn.field (complex numbers). spin_doctor.py appends to rotdyn.dat, one row per solution, the complex values of

Column Quantity 1 \(\omega_M\), mantle rotation rate 2 \(\omega_{IC}\), inner core rotation rate 3 \(\varphi\), inner core - mantle angle 4 gravitational torque \(K\varphi\) 5 viscous torque on the mantle 6 electromagnetic torque on the mantle 7 viscous torque on the inner core 8 electromagnetic torque on the inner core

The total axial angular momentum (fluid, mantle and inner core) is conserved by these equations; the fluid's own balance and the torques are written out in Angular momentum balance. spin_doctor's resid𝐋 checks the fluid's part of the balance, \(\lambda L_z\) against the torques on the boundaries. Its resid0 stays at \(10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-3}\) with rotdyn = 1, because the work done by the moving boundaries on the fluid is not included in that balance yet (see Checking the results).

docs.title: How parameters are set
docs.text:
All parameters are attributes of one object, par. Their defaults, with comments listing the available options, are in bin/params_default.py. bin/parameters.py is where a problem is set up:

from params_default import default_params, pmak, ssak
import numpy as np

par = default_params()      # every parameter at its default value

par.Ek       = 1e-6         # change only what differs from the defaults
par.magnetic = 1
...

par.set_scales()            # computes the derived parameters; call it last

par.set_scales() fills in the parameters that depend on others, unless they were set explicitly: the magnetic numbers Em, Le and Le2, the diffusion numbers Etherm and Ecomp, the buoyancy factors BV2 and BV2_comp, the time scale factor OmgTau, the resolution N and lmax, and the solver target tau. Set every parameter before this call: a change made after it does not reach the derived parameters.

All the scripts in bin/ read the parameters with from parameters import par, so the same parameters.py must be in place for every step of a run. Parameter studies set one parameter per run folder (see Many runs); the spare parameters aux1 and aux2 are recorded in params.dat and can be used, for example, to define a ramp.

The sections below follow the order of params_default.py. The magnetic boundary conditions, the background field, the rotational dynamics and the solver options have pages of their own.

docs.title: Physics switches
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning hydro 1 Include the momentum (Navier-Stokes) equation for the flow \(\mathbf{u}\). magnetic 0 Include the induction equation for the magnetic field perturbation \(\mathbf{b}\) and the Lorentz force. Needs a background field, see Background magnetic field. thermal 0 Include the heat equation and thermal buoyancy (Boussinesq). compositional 0 Include the composition equation and compositional buoyancy (Boussinesq). rotdyn 0 Let the mantle and the inner core rotate in response to axial torques, see Rotational dynamics. rotation 1 Rotating frame. With 0 the Coriolis force is left out; then use a time scale other than the rotation one (e.g. timescale = 'viscous') and set N explicitly.

docs.title: Geometry and symmetry
docs.text: Parameter Default Meaning ricb 0.35 Inner core radius. The CMB radius is 1 and is the unit of length. ricb = 0 is a full sphere. m 0 Azimuthal wave number (\(m \geq 0\)). All fields vary as \(e^{im\phi}\). symm 1 Equatorial symmetry of the flow: 1 symmetric, -1 antisymmetric. The magnetic field perturbation has symmetry symm times that of the background field, and temperature and composition follow the flow.

docs.title: Flow boundary conditions and Ekman number
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning bci 1 Flow condition at the inner core boundary (ICB): 0 stress-free, 1 no-slip (or boundary forcing). Ignored if ricb = 0. bco 1 Flow condition at the core-mantle boundary (CMB): 0 stress-free, 1 no-slip (or boundary forcing). Ek \(10^{-6}\) Ekman number \(E = \nu/\Omega L^2\).

Ek = 0 gives an inviscid problem, with only the no-penetration condition \(u_r = 0\) at the boundary. It works only for a full sphere (ricb = 0), and N must then be set by hand. A conducting inner core, a thin conducting wall with c1 \(\neq 0\), and rotdyn all need a viscous fluid and no-slip boundaries.

docs.title: Eigenvalue or forced problem
docs.text:
With forcing = 0 (the default) Kore solves the eigenvalue problem \(A\,x = \lambda B\,x\) for the free modes. Any other value selects a forced problem, solved as one linear system at the frequency forcing_frequency:

forcing Forcing Requirements 1 Tidal body force of Lin & Ogilvie (2018) \(m = 2\), symmetric 2 Boundary flow forcing bci = 1, bco = 1 3 Tidal body force of Rovira-Navarro et al. (2018) \(m\) = 0 and 2 symmetric, \(m = 1\) antisymmetric. Leaks power. 4 Test case: Lin body force with \(X(r) = (A r^2 + B/r^3)\,C\) \(m = 2\), symmetric 5 Test case: Lin body force with \(X(r) = 1/r\) \(m = 0\), symmetric 6 Radial velocity forcing at the ICB (Buffett 2010) \(m = 1\), antisymmetric 7 Longitudinal libration as boundary flow forcing \(m\) = 0 or 2, symmetric, no-slip 8 Longitudinal libration as a Poincaré body force, in the mantle frame \(m = 0\), symmetric, no-slip 9 Radial boundary flow forcing \(m = 2\), symmetric Parameter Default Meaning forcing_frequency 0 Frequency of the forcing, in the units set by timescale. Negative is prograde. forcing_amplitude_cmb 0 Forcing amplitude at the CMB. Body forces use this value. forcing_amplitude_icb 0 Forcing amplitude at the ICB. projection 1 Recorded in params.dat; not used by the current solver.

Forced problems use a direct solver and keep the amplitude set by the forcing (see Solver settings).

docs.title: Time scale
docs.text:
The equations can be written with different units of time (see Equations and scaling). The choice enters through the dimensionless rotation rate \(\Omega\tau\), OmgTau, which set_scales() sets from timescale unless OmgTau is given directly:

timescale Unit of time \(\tau\) OmgTau 'rotation' (default) \(1/\Omega\) 1 'viscous' \(L^2/\nu\) \(1/E\) 'Alfven' \(L\sqrt{\mu_0\rho}/B_0\) \(1/Le\) 'magnetic' \(L^2/\eta\) \(1/E_\eta\)

Eigenvalues, frequencies and forcing frequencies are all in these units.

docs.title: Magnetic field strength and diffusivity
docs.text:
The field strength and the magnetic diffusivity can be given in either of two ways:

  • the Elsasser number Lambda (\(\Lambda\), default 0.1) and the magnetic Prandtl number Pm (default 0.01). Then set_scales() computes the magnetic Ekman number \(E_\eta\) = Em = Ek/Pm, Le2 \(= \Lambda E_\eta\) and the Lehnert number Le \(= \sqrt{\Lambda E_\eta}\);
  • or the Lehnert number Le and the magnetic Ekman number Em directly, in which case Lambda and Pm are not used.

The Lundquist number is Le/Em. The helper functions pmak(Pm0, E0, Ek) and ssak(Lambda0, E0, Ek) in params_default.py return Pm and Lambda as power laws of Ek through the point (E0, Pm0) or (E0, Lambda0), useful to keep a path towards Earth-like values when lowering Ek.

The background field itself is chosen with B0, cnorm and related parameters (Background magnetic field), and the magnetic boundary conditions with innercore and mantle (Inner core and mantle).

docs.title: Thermal parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning Prandtl 1 Prandtl number \(Pr = \nu/\kappa\). Etherm Ek/Prandtl Thermal Ekman number. heating 'internal' Background temperature gradient, see below. Ra \(2.5168 \times 10^8\) Rayleigh number \(Ra = \alpha g_0 L^3 \Delta T/\nu\kappa\), with \(L\) the CMB radius and \(\Delta T\) the temperature scale below. BV2 -Ra*Ek**2/Prandtl Squared ratio of a reference Brunt-Väisälä frequency to the rotation rate, \(N_0^2/\Omega^2\). Set it directly for problems without diffusion, where Ra is undefined. Negative values are unstably stratified. rc, h, rsy 0.7, 0.1, -1 Transition radius, width and radial parity for 'two zone' and 'user defined'. bci_thermal, bco_thermal 1, 1 At the ICB and the CMB: 0 isothermal (\(\theta = 0\)), 1 fixed heat flux (\(\partial_r\theta = 0\)). heating Background gradient \(dT/dr\) Temperature scale 'internal' \(-\beta r\) (uniform internal heating) \(\beta r_o^2\) 'differential' \(-\beta r^{-2}\), with \(\beta = (T_i - T_o)\, r_i r_o / (r_o - r_i)\) \(T_i - T_o\) 'two zone' \(K\,\)ut.twozone(r): a neutral inner zone and a stratified outer zone joined by a tanh step at rc (Vidal et al. 2015) \(-r_o K\) 'user defined' \(K\,\)ut.BVprof(r), a function you edit in bin/utils.py (by default \(\propto r\)) \(-r_o K\)

The profiles are expanded in Chebyshev polynomials to the tolerance tol_tc (default \(10^{-6}\)).

docs.title: Compositional parameters
docs.text: These mirror the thermal ones: Schmidt (Schmidt number \(Sc = \nu/D\), default 1), Ecomp (default Ek/Schmidt), comp_background ('internal' or 'differential'), Ra_comp (compositional Rayleigh number, default 0), BV2_comp (default -Ra_comp*Ek**2/Schmidt), rcc, hc, rsyc, and bci_compositional, bco_compositional (0 fixed composition, 1 fixed flux).

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning ncpus 4 Number of MPI processes for submatrices.py and assemble.py. N Ncheb(Ek) Number of Chebyshev polynomials in radius, in the fluid. Must be even for a full sphere. g 1 Approximate ratio \(l_{max}/N\). lmax from N, g, ncpus, m Largest spherical-harmonic degree, \(2\,n_{cpu} \lfloor gN/2n_{cpu} \rfloor + m - 1\). Set by hand, it must be even if \(m\) is odd, and \(l_{max} - m + 1\) must be divisible by \(2\,n_{cpu}\). N_cic 64 Chebyshev polynomials for the field inside a conducting inner core. lmax_cic lmax Largest degree inside a conducting inner core.

How to choose N and lmax, and how to check that they are large enough, is explained in Solver settings and Output and postprocessing.

docs.title: Target and eigensolver
docs.text:
Parameter Default Meaning rtau, itau 0, 1 Real (damping) and imaginary (frequency) parts of the target \(\tau\) = rtau + 1j*itau. The eigensolver returns the modes closest to it. A positive frequency is retrograde. which_eigenpairs 'TM' Which eigenvalues SLEPc returns. First letter: L largest, S smallest, T closest to the target. Second letter: M magnitude, R real part, I imaginary part. Use 'TM' with shift-and-invert. nev 3 Number of eigenvalues to compute. maxit 50 Maximum number of restarts of the eigensolver (iterations for forced problems). tol \(10^{-16}\) Convergence tolerance of the solver. track_target 0 With 1, set_scales() reads rtau and itau from the first two numbers in a file track_target, e.g. to follow a mode along a parameter path.

The PETSc, SLEPc and MUMPS options (petsc_opts) and the pre-scaling switch (prescale) are described in Solver settings.

docs.title: Solver settings
docs.text:
The solver options are defined, with their defaults, in bin/params_default.py, and can be changed in bin/parameters.py (e.g. par.petsc_opts['eps_balance'] = 'twoside'). Most of them are collected in the petsc_opts dictionary, which solve_nopp.py loads into PETSc's options database at start-up. Each key is a PETSc/SLEPc/MUMPS option name without the leading -. Only the group that matches the problem type is used: eps_* and st_* options for eigenvalue problems (forcing = 0), and ksp_*, pc_* and mat_* options for forced problems. Any option given on the command line takes precedence over petsc_opts, for example:

mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve_nopp.py -st_mat_mumps_icntl_35 0

The defaults described below are the recommended settings for production runs.

docs.title: Eigenvalue problems
docs.text:
Eigensolver. solve_nopp.py solves the generalized eigenvalue problem \(A\,x = \lambda B\,x\) with SLEPc's default Krylov-Schur method. It looks for nev eigenvalues (default 3) closest to the target \(\tau\) = rtau + 1j*itau, as selected by which_eigenpairs = 'TM' (target magnitude). The real part of \(\tau\) is the damping and the imaginary part the frequency of the modes sought. tol and maxit set SLEPc's convergence tolerance and maximum number of restarts. The size of the Krylov search space (eps_ncv) is left at SLEPc's default.

Shift-and-invert ('st_type': 'sinvert'). SLEPc does not work with \(A\) and \(B\) directly but with \((A-\tau B)^{-1}B\). The eigenvalues closest to \(\tau\) become the largest ones of this operator, so the method converges in a few iterations even deep inside the spectrum. Each iteration needs one solve with \(A-\tau B\), so that matrix is factorized once, at the start.

Direct LU with MUMPS ('st_pc_factor_mat_solver_type': 'mumps'). The factorization of \(A-\tau B\) is done by the parallel sparse direct solver MUMPS. Factorization takes most of the run time and memory.

  • 'st_mat_mumps_cntl_1': 1e-8 is MUMPS's relative pivoting threshold. MUMPS's default (0.01) makes it delay many pivots on Kore's matrices, so large problems run out of workspace (error INFOG(1) = -9) and the factorization is slow. A small threshold avoids this, while still guarding against an exactly zero pivot. Do not raise it above about 1e-8 when block low-rank factorization is on (see the next item): larger values can spoil the eigenvectors of large problems.
  • 'st_mat_mumps_icntl_35': 2 switches on block low-rank (BLR) factorization. MUMPS compresses blocks of the factors that are numerically of low rank, which reduces both memory and factorization time considerably for large matrices.
  • 'st_mat_mumps_cntl_7': 1e-14 is the BLR compression tolerance. It is set close to machine precision so that BLR does not reduce accuracy. Looser values (e.g. 1e-12 or 1e-10) save a little more memory but degrade the eigenvectors.
  • MUMPS's own row and column scaling of the matrix (icntl_8) is left at its default and should stay on.

Pre-scaling (prescale = 1, the default). The rows and columns of Kore's matrices differ in size by many orders of magnitude. With prescale = 1, solve_nopp.py equilibrates \(A-\tau B\) before the factorization (Ruiz scaling: rows and columns are scaled repeatedly until their largest entries are all of order one). It then solves the scaled problem \((D_r A D_c)\,y = \lambda\,(D_r B D_c)\,y\). The eigenvalues are the same, and the eigenvectors are mapped back, \(x = D_c\,y\), before they are written to disk. Pre-scaling reduces the condition number of the matrix by many orders of magnitude and gives more accurate eigenvectors, at the cost of a few seconds. It is used for eigenvalue problems only. Set par.prescale = 0 in parameters.py to switch it off. SLEPc's -eps_true_residual option does not converge together with pre-scaling at tol = 1e-15 or below.

Eigenvector normalisation. Eigenvectors are only defined up to a complex factor. Before they are written, each eigenvector is scaled so that its total kinetic plus magnetic energy, integrated over the fluid outer core, equals 1, using the same definitions as spin_doctor.py. Energies, dissipations and torques reported by spin_doctor.py therefore refer to a mode of unit total energy. The complex phase is left as returned by SLEPc.

Error report ('eps_error_relative': '::ascii_info_detail'). After the solve, solve_nopp.py prints each eigenvalue with its relative residual \(\|Ax-\lambda Bx\|/\|\lambda x\|\). With prescale = 1 this residual refers to the scaled problem. A small value shows that SLEPc converged, but it does not guarantee an accurate eigenvector. Always check the residuals computed by spin_doctor.py (see Checking the results).

Optional settings. These are commented out in petsc_opts and can be switched on when needed:

  • 'eps_balance': 'twoside' balances the matrices before the solve. It gives cleaner eigenvalues for final runs, at roughly 50% more run time.
  • 'st_mat_mumps_icntl_14' increases MUMPS's workspace (in percent). It is only needed if INFOG(1) = -9 still appears.
  • 'st_mat_mumps_icntl_22': 1 stores the factors out of core, on disk, which roughly halves the memory needed. Set 'st_mat_mumps_ooc_tmpdir' to a directory on a real disk, not on a memory-backed /tmp.
  • 'st_mat_mumps_icntl_28': 2 with 'st_mat_mumps_icntl_29': 2 makes MUMPS compute its fill-reducing ordering in parallel, with ParMETIS.

docs.title: Forced problems
docs.text: For forced problems (forcing > 0) Kore solves a single linear system. The defaults are a direct solve: 'ksp_type': 'preonly', 'pc_type': 'lu' and 'pc_factor_mat_solver_type': 'mumps'. Iterative solvers (PETSc's default GMRES with ILU) do not converge reliably on these matrices. If MUMPS reports INFOG(1) = -9, uncomment 'mat_mumps_cntl_1'. Pre-scaling and the energy normalisation are not applied: the solution keeps the amplitude set by the forcing.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Unless N is set in parameters.py, par.set_scales() sets the Chebyshev truncation to Ncheb(Ek) (in params_default.py), and the spherical-harmonic truncation lmax follows from N (with g = 1, lmax = N - 1 for m = 0). Ncheb grows as \(E_k^{-0.242}\); for example it gives N = 136, 232, 400 and 688 at \(E_k\) = 1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8 and 1e-9. It was obtained for a torsional-mode problem. Other problems (stronger fields, other boundary conditions, buoyancy) may need a higher resolution. Keep lmax close to N: a too small lmax changes the eigenvalues without showing up in spin_doctor's residuals.

Memory is usually the limit. It grows roughly as \(N^{2.2}\) and is larger at lower Ekman numbers: with the default settings (BLR on, 8 processes) a run at N = 688 (\(E_k\) = 1e-9) needs about 34 GB, and N = 1200 (\(E_k\) = 1e-10, extrapolated) would need about 115 to 120 GB. The out-of-core option above roughly halves it.

A conducting inner core has its own resolution, N_cic (see Inner core and mantle).

To check that a solution is accurate, use spin_doctor's residuals, as described in Checking the results.
